label: geometry batch 2 — congruence criteria and angle sum

widget.prompt: AB = CB, so the legs are locked equal at 6. Drag the apex angle to 50° and watch the two base angles the whole way — can you ever make ∠A and ∠C disagree?
widget.constraintFeedback: You released the lock, so the legs are no longer equal — the base angles are now reading a different triangle than the one the proof is about. Re-lock them.
widget.successFeedback: They never disagree. With AB = CB and D the midpoint of AC, the two halves share three pairs of equal sides — SSS — so △ABD ≅ △CBD, and ∠A = ∠C follows by CPCTC. The lab shows the conclusion is forced at every apex angle, not just this one.
widget.criterionFeedback: SSA does not lock a triangle. The proof uses three pairs of equal SIDES: AB = CB, the shared BD, and AD = DC from the midpoint.
widget.angleFeedback: Right criterion — now bring the apex angle to 50°.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Drag through several apex angles before checking. The claim is that ∠A = ∠C ALWAYS, which one position cannot show.

widget.prompt: AB = CB locks the legs equal at 7, and BD bisects the apex angle. Drag the apex to 60° and watch what happens to AD and CD.
widget.constraintFeedback: The legs are no longer locked equal, so AB = CB has stopped being true and the proof no longer applies. Re-lock them.
widget.successFeedback: AD = CD at every apex angle. The bisector splits the apex into two equal angles, the legs are equal, and BD is shared — two sides and the included angle, SAS — so △ABD ≅ △CBD and AD = CD by CPCTC.
widget.criterionFeedback: SSA is the ambiguous case. Here the equal angle sits BETWEEN the two equal sides, which is SAS.
widget.angleFeedback: Right criterion — now bring the apex angle to 60°.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Try several apex angles before checking; the theorem claims AD = CD for all of them.

widget.prompt: AB = AC locks the legs equal at 8, and BD = CD is given. Drag the apex to 70°, then decide what AD is doing in this figure.
widget.constraintFeedback: The legs came unlocked, so AB = AC is no longer true and the overlap argument breaks. Re-lock them.
widget.successFeedback: AD is the shared side — the part both triangles own. With AB = AC, BD = CD and AD common, that is SSS, so △ABD ≅ △ACD and ∠BAD = ∠CAD. The shared side is free evidence, and spotting it is the whole skill in an overlapping figure.
widget.criterionFeedback: Look again at what the givens actually are — every piece of this argument is a SIDE: the two equal legs, the two equal segments, and the one the triangles share. No angle is given anywhere.
widget.angleFeedback: Right criterion — now bring the apex angle to 70°.
widget.evidenceFeedback: Move through several positions first. The shared side AD stays shared at every one of them, which is why the argument does not depend on the picture.

widget.prompt: Two triangles each have angles of 40° and 75°. Drag corner C until angle A reads the third angle they must share — and watch the total the whole way.
widget.successFeedback: 65°, because 40 + 75 + 65 = 180. Notice what the readouts did while you dragged: every angle changed, the total never did. That invariant is the whole reason AA works — fix two angles and the third has nowhere else to go, so the shapes must match.
widget.targetFeedback: Not 65° yet. The other two angles are 40° and 75°, and all three must total 180°.
widget.invariantFeedback: Watch the total as you drag, not just angle A. It reads 180° at every position, and that is the fact the AA criterion rests on.

widget.prompt: The triangle has A = 40° and B = 65°. Drag corner C until angle A reads the size of the remaining angle C.
widget.successFeedback: C = 75°, since 40 + 65 + 75 = 180. This matters before any Law of Sines work: the rule pairs each angle with the side opposite it, so the third angle has to be found first or the largest side has no angle to pair with.
widget.targetFeedback: Not there yet. A and B are 40° and 65°, and the three angles total 180°.
widget.invariantFeedback: Keep an eye on the total while dragging — it stays at 180°, which is what lets you find any angle from the other two.

refusals.title: Circumscribed Figures
refusals.why: A circle of radius 6 inscribed in a square, find the square's perimeter. Checked against the catalogue: circleAngleExplore models angle relationships (central|inscribed|tangentChord|cyclic); circleMeasureExplore models chordDistance|tangentLength|arcSector|radiusScale; scaledCircleLab asks realRadius|circumferenceCoef|areaCoef. None represents a circle inscribed in a polygon. Refused.

refusals.title: Angles Inside & Outside
refusals.why: The step computes the angle between two tangents from an EXTERNAL point — half the difference of the intercepted arcs. circleAngleExplore's modes are central | inscribed | tangentChord | cyclic; the two-secant/two-tangent external case and the two-chord internal case are both absent. I expected this course to fit circleAngleExplore and it does not: the circle lessons still at Tier C are precisely the ones outside its four modes. Refused.

refusals.title: Power of a Point
refusals.why: Every chord through an interior point splits into pieces with a constant product. No engine models power of a point; circleMeasureExplore's chordDistance is the distance from centre to chord, a different quantity. Refused.

refusals.title: Circumcenter & Incenter
refusals.why: Triangle centers. Searched the full manip>=2 catalogue: no engine represents a triangle centre or the concurrency of perpendicular bisectors, angle bisectors, medians or altitudes. triangleConstraintLab constrains side/angle criteria; triangleAngleLab drags a vertex and reads angles. Refused.

refusals.title: Centroid & Orthocenter
refusals.why: Same as tc-04-01 — the 2:1 centroid ratio and the orthocenter have no representation in any registered engine. Refused.

refusals.title: Choosing the Right Center
refusals.why: Sorts the four centres by the lines that define them — a classification over a concept no engine models, so the sort has nothing manipulable behind it. Refused.
